articles.title: Who Benefits from Citizenship? Varying Effects of Naturalization Decisions in the Early-Twentieth-Century United States
articles.authors: Peter Catron, Nathan I. Hoffmann, Mingze Li
articles.abstract: Citizenship acquisition is widely viewed as a mechanism for improving economic outcomes, yet little is known about whether its benefits are distributed evenly. This article examines the varied returns to naturalization in the early-twentieth-century United States, assessing whether naturalization uniformly benefits all immigrants or is especially impactful for those already positioned to profit. Using naturalization records from New York City’s Southern District in the early 1900s, we construct a novel historical dataset for 1,947 immigrants who declared their intent to naturalize. By linking these records to U.S. census data from 1920, 1930, and 1940, we are able to observe immigrants’ characteristics at the point when they make naturalization decisions and to track their outcomes over time. Our findings reveal that immigrants who completed the naturalization process attained significantly higher occupational status than those who initiated but did not complete naturalization. In addition, citizenship is most transformative for those facing the greatest disadvantages. Additional analyses corroborate these findings in linked full-count census data for the entire United States. Citizenship confers occupational advantages not only through formal rights but as a resource that enables claims-making in the labor market, with greater returns to less advantaged immigrants.

articles.title: Beyond economic bargaining power? Work-related internal migration and subjective well-being in couples
articles.authors: Elias Hofmann, Nico Stawarz, Nicolai Netz, Heiko Rüger
articles.abstract: Bargaining theory posits that both partners’ utility shapes couples’ migration decisions. Yet, most empirical tests focus on individual incomes, thus overlooking non-economic factors in couples’ deliberations about spatial mobility. We argue that considering holistic indicators of utility, such as subjective well-being, can advance our understanding of couples’ decision-making. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP, 1991–2021) and fixed effects panel regressions, we analyze changes in life satisfaction following work-related internal migration on both individual and dyadic levels. Moreover, we examine whether these changes depend on shifts in partners’ economic bargaining power (EBP, defined as female partners’ share of total household labor income), thereby evaluating the common assumption that couples’ bargaining centers around income. Our results show that, on average, both partners experience increases in their life satisfaction following migration. Distinguishing whether women’s EBP remains unchanged, decreases, or increases with migration, we find that women’s life satisfaction gains are only weakly related to changes in their EBP. In contrast, men’s life satisfaction only increases if their partner’s EBP decreases or remains unchanged, but not if it increases—a pattern consistent with the notion of gendered expectations about the within-couple income distribution hampering men’s well-being gains. Overall, our findings suggest that well-being is an important factor in couples’ migration decision-making and that income-based measures of bargaining power provide only an incomplete account of partners’ bargaining positions.

articles.title: Review of “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment”
Music divisions and cultural hierarchy in China: how transnational, political, and historical forces shape symbolic boundaries
articles.abstract: This study maps the division of music in China and examines the mechanisms underlying its formation. Methodologically, it introduces multidimensional item response theory (MIRT), a latent-trait approach rarely used in cultural sociology, to identify the social divisions of taste before examining their social stratification through regression analysis. The findings reveal six taste profiles: high-status traditional music; pop music stratified into middlebrow Hong Kong and Taiwan classics, unstratified mainstream Chinese pop, and low-status local music; and foreign music divided into high-status selective forms and unstratified trendy foreign pop. These divisions do not cleanly align with genre categories, a highbrow–lowbrow hierarchy, or omnivore–univore patterns in established accounts. Instead, they reveal dual forms of high-status taste—state-consecrated heritage and cosmopolitan selective foreign pop—reflecting a multidimensional structure organized around region of origin, historical prestige, cohort, and popularity. More broadly, this study reveals how cultural stratification in China extends beyond Bourdieusian models centered on domestic field competition to encompass global flows, state-directed legitimation, and historical local trajectories. These findings extend theories of cultural distinction beyond the assumptions derived from dominant Western liberal-market societies and offer a framework for understanding how cultural hierarchies are constituted across wider national contexts.

articles.title: Workplace authority in China: gender, parenthood, and work sectors
articles.abstract: Workplace authority is a key individual and organizational resource to which women typically have more limited access than men. Yet, less is known about how parenthood shapes this gender disparity and how the relationship varies across employment regimes. Drawing on nationally representative, longitudinal data from the China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022), I examine within-person changes in women’s and men’s access to supervisory authority following parenthood, with particular attention to variation across the state and private sectors. Fixed-effects results show that, overall, women’s likelihood of holding authority declines after becoming mothers, especially after having two or more children, whereas men experience little change. These dynamics differ by work sector. A considerable motherhood penalty is concentrated in the private sector, whereas a fatherhood premium emerges only in the state sector. Parenthood therefore widens the gender gap in authority in both sectors through distinct patterns. These findings suggest that employment regimes condition the gendered meanings of parenthood and how they translate into access to authority. In China, the state sector’s formal protections may buffer motherhood-related disadvantages, whereas its male-dominated hierarchy and pronatalist agendas may sustain fatherhood-related rewards.

articles.title: Workplace Segregation by Ethnicity and Gender in Israel: The Role of Local Labor Markets, 2000 to 2015
articles.abstract: The present research joins the growing body of organizational studies that explore workplace segregation. Using unique longitudinal employer-employee data that cover the entire Israeli economy from 2000 to 2015, this article suggests three distinct contributions to the literature. First, it describes previously unexplored patterns and trends in workplace segregation in Israel, uncovering the extreme ethnic segregation between Jews and Arabs, as well as high gender segregation; both are stable over time. Second, it shows that ethnic and gender statuses intersect and produce divergent patterns of segregation over time. Finally, the study demonstrates that the uneven distribution of the workforce across local labor markets (defined as industries within regions) constitutes an important structural source of workplace segregation. At the same time, segregation between workplaces within local labor markets accounts for most of the overall segregation, pointing to the decisive role of organizational processes in shaping workplace segregation. The study also illustrates the potential of nationwide employer-employee data and the utility of the Theil entropy index as a prominent segregation measure for investigating workplace segregation as a complex, context-contingent phenomenon.

articles.title: Internal Migration and Immobility in Early Adulthood
articles.abstract: How do life-course events and roles affect internal migration in young adulthood in the United States? Building on and extending existing explanations, the authors proposes that life-course events typically disrupt lives, increasing mobility, whereas the roles that subsequently follow tend to tie people to place. Using monthly data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997, the authors empirically distinguish between life-course events and roles in young adulthood across work, education, marital, and parental domains and assess the effects of each on interstate moves. The findings show that events and roles have opposing effects within life-course domains and in a similar pattern across domains, indicating that their effects not only are due to domain-specific factors but also reflect a set of larger principles across domains. The findings also demonstrate the importance of accounting for events and roles in combination rather than in isolation of each other.
